what.text: Kratom is a tropical tree (Mitragyna speciosa) native to Southeast Asia. Products made from its leaves are sold in the US online and in stores. FDA says kratom is often used to self-treat pain, coughing, diarrhea, anxiety and depression, opioid use disorder and opioid withdrawal. An estimated 1.7 million Americans aged 12 and older used kratom in 2021.

src.label: FDA, “FDA and Kratom”

what.text: Kratom contains more than 50 alkaloids. Most research looks at mitragynine, the main one, and 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH). Both bind to the same brain receptors (mu-opioid receptors) as opioid drugs such as codeine. Mitragynine also acts on serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine and kappa-opioid systems.

src.label: FDA, “FDA and Kratom”

what.text: 7-OH makes up less than 2% of the alkaloids in natural kratom leaves, but it is much more potent at the mu-opioid receptor than mitragynine, and more potent than morphine. It can be made from mitragynine in one chemical step and is also formed from mitragynine in the body. FDA distinguishes concentrated 7-OH products, sold as tablets, gummies, drink mixes and shots, from the natural leaf.

what.text: Researchers report that kratom is used in the US for energy and to self-manage pain and mood. DEA reports that unapproved 7-OH products were marketed for pain, relaxation and “mood enhancement.”

what.text: No kratom or kratom-alkaloid drug is FDA approved. FDA says kratom cannot be lawfully sold as a dietary supplement or added to food.

research.text: A few small controlled studies have given kratom or mitragynine to people, mostly to test safety, blood levels and abuse potential over days or weeks. None of the studies found tested it as a treatment for depression or anxiety. FDA says there are few well-designed human studies.
FDA: “Although there are published animal studies with kratom extracts, there are few published reports from well-designed scientific studies where kratom was administered to humans.”

src.label: FDA, “FDA and Kratom”

research.title: Single and 15 daily doses of dried leaf, healthy adults

facts.v: 116 healthy adults aged 18 to 55 who had not used kratom for at least 12 months (49 kratom, 67 placebo)
500 to 4,000 mg of dried kratom leaf powder (6.65 to 53.2 mg mitragynine), once and then once a day for 15 days
side effects, abuse-related effects and withdrawal

research.found: No serious adverse events or deaths. Side effects rose with dose: dizziness, nausea and feeling relaxed after single doses; headache, feeling hot, raised liver enzyme (ALT) and nausea after repeated doses. Drug-effect ratings rose only at the highest single dose, and no one met the threshold for meaningful opioid withdrawal. The trial was funded by a company, one author works for that company, and some authors consult for kratom industry groups.

src.label: Huestis et al., Ther Drug Monit, 2026
Coe et al., Drug Test Anal, 2026

research.title: Single doses in people with opioid experience

facts.v: double-blind, placebo-controlled, single ascending doses; first author from FDA
40 recreational drug users with opioid experience who were otherwise healthy (6 kratom and 2 placebo per dose group)
a single dose of 1, 3, 8, 10 or 12 g of leaf kratom with trace 7-OH
pupil size, subjective effects, blood levels, heart tracing (ECG), labs and suicidality

research.found: No deaths or serious adverse events. Sleepiness, vomiting and nausea were most common. Doses of 3 g or more narrowed the pupils, an opioid-like effect. The 12 g dose raised ratings of “drug liking,” “good effects” and “high.”

src.label: Reissig et al., J Clin Psychopharmacol, 2026
ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06072170 (single ascending doses of kratom)

research.title: Pure mitragynine, healthy volunteers

facts.v: 15 healthy volunteers (8 in part A, 7 in part B)
single doses of 5, 10 and 20 mg (part A) or 40 mg (part B) of mitragynine
vital signs, drug experience, attention and thinking tests, and pain tolerance over 7 hours

research.found: Most measures did not change at any dose. The 5 mg dose raised ratings of arousal and attention and some attention-task scores. The 40 mg dose raised ratings of amnesia and caused mild psychiatric symptoms. Side effects were mild and short-lived.

src.label: Prevete et al., Psychopharmacology, 2025

research.title: Pain tolerance in regular users

facts.v: randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind; kratom drink and matched placebo drinks during a 1-day stay
26 men, average age 24, who had used kratom daily for about 6 years
pain tolerance in a cold-water hand test, and withdrawal signs

research.found: Pain tolerance rose 60 minutes after the kratom drink (from 11.2 to 24.9 seconds on average) and did not change after placebo. No withdrawal signs were seen in the 10 to 20 hours without kratom.

src.label: Vicknasingam et al., Yale J Biol Med, 2020

research.title: Kratom use and moment-to-moment anxiety and sadness

facts.v: secondary analysis; people rated their mood on their phones several times a day for 15 days
anxiety and sadness in the 3 hours after kratom use compared with no use

research.found: Kratom use was linked with small drops in anxiety and, less clearly, sadness. It was not a randomized trial, so it cannot show cause and effect; the authors say randomized trials are needed. One author reports consulting and paid expert-witness work.

us.text: Not FDA approved. FDA says kratom is not lawfully marketed in the US as a drug, a dietary supplement or a food ingredient. Kratom and mitragynine are not federally controlled, and as of November 1, 2026, 7-OH is not yet in Schedule I; DEA has proposed to schedule 7-OH above a set level. Three related lab-made compounds have been in Schedule I since August 2026.

items.text: “There are no prescription or over-the-counter drug products containing kratom or its known alkaloids that are legally on the market in the U.S.”

items.text: FDA asked DEA to control certain 7-OH products under the Controlled Substances Act, aiming at concentrated 7-OH and not at natural kratom leaf products. FDA said there are no FDA-approved 7-OH drugs and that 7-OH is not lawful in dietary supplements or food. In June 2025 FDA sent warning letters to seven companies over 7-OH products.

src.label: DEA, notice of intent: 7-hydroxymitragynine above a threshold (Federal Register 2026-13580)

items.text: DEA withdrew the July notice and issued a new one, based on an HHS letter of October 8, 2026. 7-OH and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl would be in Schedule I when either one, or both together, is above 1 mg per gram (solids) or 1 mg per millilitre (liquids), or when the ratio of mitragynine to them is under 100 to 1. The order is to be published on or after November 13, 2026. DEA says neither HHS nor DEA has found these substances safe below the threshold.

us.text: DEA's October 2026 notice says ten states (Alabama, Arkansas, Connecticut, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Tennessee, Vermont and Wisconsin) have prohibited 7-OH consumption; that some states, such as Arizona, Colorado, South Carolina and Texas, limit 7-OH content; that 19 states have passed a kratom consumer protection act; and that some localities in other states ban kratom. This is DEA's summary; the state laws themselves were not opened for this page.

after.text: Kratom, mitragynine and 7-OH are not named on the WADA Prohibited List for 2026 or 2027, and not on the 2027 Monitoring Program. The narcotics class (S7) names specific substances, such as morphine and oxycodone, and mitragynine is not among them. WADA’s class S0 bans at all times any pharmacological substance not covered elsewhere on the List and with no current approval by any government health regulator for human therapeutic use. The lists do not say whether kratom or its alkaloids fall under S0.

side.text: FDA warns of liver toxicity, seizures and substance use disorder. Kratom's alkaloids can cause opioid-like effects, including breathing problems that may lead to death. Deaths with kratom have mostly involved other drugs as well.

items.text: possible opioid-like effects include sedation, nausea and vomiting, constipation, physical dependence and withdrawal, and respiratory depression that may lead to death. Cases of substance use disorder and of withdrawal in newborns after kratom use in pregnancy have been reported. Some kratom products were contaminated with Salmonella or heavy metals.

src.label: FDA, “FDA and Kratom”

items.text: FDA says deaths have been linked to kratom in rare cases, usually with other drugs, so kratom's role is unclear. CDC found kratom on toxicology in 152 of 27,338 overdose deaths (0.56%) in 27 states from July 2016 to December 2017; it was ruled a cause of death in 91. Only 7 had no other substance detected. Fentanyl was the most common other drug.

src.label: FDA, “FDA and Kratom”

items.text: 660 kratom calls. Common signs were fast heart rate (25%), agitation (24%), drowsiness (19%), nausea (15%) and high blood pressure (12%). 7.4% had a major (life-threatening) outcome. 72% of callers were male; median age 28.

surprises: DEA tried to schedule kratom's two main alkaloids in 2016 and withdrew within six weeks; ten years later it scheduled three 7-OH-related compounds and proposed scheduling 7-OH itself, but not the natural leaf.
The HHS threshold for 7-OH is designed to leave products closer to natural kratom leaf outside Schedule I, while DEA says this is not a finding that they are safe.
